concepts.title: Today's work
concepts.hook: The train is late and a project is due next week. You can plan for next week, but what needs your hands now?
concepts.rule: Carnegie's day by day frame puts today's work in view. Plan for later, then return to the next task. It is one way to think, not a cure for worry. If worry keeps getting in the way, talk with a doctor or counsellor.

claims.text: Carnegie's advice in Part One, chapter 1: give today's tasks your care, while leaving room to plan for tomorrow.
What research says: In one lab test, people asked to worry about a real problem came up with weaker answers than people asked to think about it in a plain way.
Carnegie's day by day idea still leaves a place for a real plan. The point is to act on what can be done now.

options.text: Set a date to renew it.

options.text: Ignore the date until the pass stops working.

options.text: A plan can guide today's task.

misconceptions.correction: A guess can go on a later list. A small task can be done now.

misconceptions.name: This means no planning
misconceptions.correction: A plan is welcome. Put its next action on today's list when the time comes.

concepts.title: A plan for the worst case
concepts.hook: A supplier may be late. An anxious guess can grow fast. What is the actual worst case, and what could you do next?
concepts.rule: Name the worst case in plain terms, allow that it may happen, then look for a way to make it less costly. This is a planning frame, not a promise. If worry stays with you, a doctor or counsellor can help you talk it through.

claims.text: Carnegie's advice in Part One, chapter 2: write down the worst result you could face, rather than let a vague fear grow.
Carnegie then asks readers to make room for that result as a real chance. This does not mean they have to welcome it.
Carnegie's last move is to look for a step that could improve the result. The plan may still need help from others.

What research says: In a study of adults without a diagnosis, three ways to reassess a feared event lowered its estimated likelihood compared with a control task. It did not test Carnegie's three-step plan.

options.text: A claim that the goods are here.
options.feedback: That would hide the real risk. A useful plan starts with the possible shortfall.

items.stem: A class event may move indoors due to rain. Which thought allows for that chance?

options.feedback: The hall plan makes room for rain while the outdoor plan can still go ahead.

options.text: Act as if rain is out of the question.
options.feedback: The rain may come. Denying that chance leaves the event with no indoor place.

items.stem: A neighbour says this method means giving up on a delayed parcel. Which reading fits?

options.text: Ask for a new date and make a backup.
options.feedback: The delay is faced as a chance, and there is still a useful step to take.
Accepting a chance of delay does not close off a call or a backup plan.

items.stem: In a worst-case plan, three notes name steps that could help and two repeat the fear. How many notes belong in the action list?

options.feedback: The three steps can guide an action. The other two restate the fear without a task.
Repeating a fear adds no new task. Keep the action list for steps you can try.

misconceptions.name: Vague fear is a plan
misconceptions.correction: A plan names a real risk and a possible step. A broad fear names neither.

misconceptions.name: Acceptance means giving up
misconceptions.correction: Making room for a possible loss can go with trying to reduce it.

concepts.title: Get the facts first
concepts.hook: A fee notice looks wrong. Before you plan for a loss, what does the notice say about the amount and due date?
concepts.rule: Carnegie's next part starts with facts, a choice, and a step. Keep a fact separate from a guess, then act on what the facts support. If a fact is missing, make finding it the next task.

claims.text: Carnegie's advice in Part Two, chapter 4: get the facts first. Then choose what to do.
What research says: In one lab test, people asked to worry about a real problem gave weaker answers than people asked to think about it in a plain way.
Carnegie then asks readers to decide what to do and start. A missing fact can make a fact check the next step.

concepts.title: Useful work
concepts.hook: A canteen order is late. There is time to check the order and time to fold the table covers. Which task is real work now?
concepts.rule: Carnegie proposes keeping busy with a useful task when a thought keeps circling. The task still needs to matter; a full day alone is no cure. Choose work that matters, and return to any open concern at its set time.

claims.text: Carnegie's advice in Part Three, chapter 6: give your time to useful work when worry keeps circling.
What research says: A small study tested a set time for worry. The people taught that method reported less worry than the comparison group. It is an early result, not a cure.
Carnegie's point is to keep a hand on a real task. That leaves room to return to an open concern at a set time.

concepts.title: Small things in scale
concepts.hook: A shop sign has one uneven letter. It can be fixed, but does it need the same care as the wrong price on the bill?
concepts.rule: Carnegie asks us to stop giving small irritations the space of large problems. Check the true cost before you act. A small cost still deserves a fix when it affects someone.

claims.text: Carnegie's advice in Part Three, chapter 7: do not let a small irritation take the whole day.
Carnegie asks readers to look at the true size of a small event before giving it more time.
A small error can still need a fix. Carnegie's point is about the time and weight we give it.
What research says: A study of daily hassles found that the minor events people reported differed by setting and tended to recur over time. Small does not always mean negligible.
